Pregnancy

Best Sleeping Position During Pregnancy by Trimester

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The best sleeping position during pregnancy is on your side, and it matters most from 28 weeks onward. Before that, in the first and second trimesters, any position that feels comfortable is fine, including your back and your stomach. If you wake up on your back later in pregnancy, do not panic: the position you fall asleep in is the one that counts, so simply roll onto your side and settle back to sleep. This guide walks through what changes each trimester and how to stay comfortable on your side.

Why side sleeping matters from 28 weeks

From around 28 weeks, the advice becomes specific: go to sleep on your side. When you lie flat on your back in later pregnancy, the weight of the uterus can press on the large blood vessels that run behind it, which can reduce blood flow to you and to the baby. UK guidance from the NHS links falling asleep on the back in the third trimester with a higher risk of stillbirth. That sounds frightening, so keep it in proportion: the overall risk is small, and settling onto your side at bedtime and after night wakings is a simple, concrete way to lower it further.

The reason guidance focuses on the position you fall asleep in is practical: it is the position you hold longest, and it is the only one you can actually control. Everyone moves during sleep, and pregnant bodies are no exception. If you wake up on your back, this is not an emergency and it does not mean you have harmed your baby. Roll onto your side, get comfortable, and go back to sleep. Many people find their body starts waking them naturally when they end up flat, with a vague ache or a restless feeling. Treat that as a helpful nudge, not a warning sign.

Early pregnancy: sleep in whatever position works

In the first trimester, sleep position is genuinely a non-issue. The uterus is still small and sits low in the pelvis, protected by bone, so your back, your stomach, and either side are all fine. If you are exhausted and queasy in early pregnancy, permission to sleep however you can is worth having in writing: comfort wins. Stomach sleeping does not squash the baby. The muscular wall of the uterus and the amniotic fluid around the baby provide real cushioning, so you can stay a front sleeper for as long as it feels good, usually well into the second trimester.

Most people give up stomach sleeping somewhere in the second trimester, not because it becomes dangerous but because sleeping on a growing bump feels like sleeping on a ball. That transition is a useful moment to start practicing side sleeping, even though the 28 week advice has not kicked in yet. Habits formed at 20 weeks make the third trimester easier. Some people also notice that lying flat on the back starts to feel unpleasant earlier, with dizziness or a faint feeling. That sensation is the same blood vessel pressure at work, and shifting onto your side usually settles it within a minute or two.

Left side, right side, and what actually matters

The left side is often suggested first because the largest vein returning blood to your heart runs slightly to the right of your spine, so lying on the left keeps the uterus off it most completely. Some clinicians also mention that left side lying may support blood flow to the placenta and the kidneys. That said, mainstream guidance treats side sleeping as the goal, not left side sleeping specifically. Falling asleep on your right side is acceptable, and current guidance treats either side as safe for going to sleep. If your left hip aches or your left shoulder complains, switch. A comfortable right side beats a miserable left side.

You also do not need to hold a rigid position all night, and you could not even if you tried. Switching sides when a hip gets sore is normal and fine. You do not have to be perfectly perpendicular to the mattress either: a relaxed position where your body is tilted toward one side, supported by a pillow behind your back, still counts as side sleeping. What you are avoiding is lying flat on your back for long stretches in late pregnancy. Think of it as a direction to lean, not a pose to perform, and let comfort settle the details night by night.

A pillow setup that keeps you on your side

You can build a solid setup with three ordinary pillows. Place one between your knees, with your knees bent, to line up your hips and ease pressure on your lower back. Tuck a second under the side of your bump so its weight is carried by the pillow instead of pulling on your skin and back muscles. Wedge the third behind your back, snug against you, so rolling flat feels blocked rather than easy. If nighttime heartburn bothers you, raising your head and shoulders a little on an extra pillow can take the edge off. That is the whole system: knees, bump, back.

A full length pregnancy pillow does the same job in one piece. With a U shaped pillow, rest your head at the curve, hug one arm of the U, slide it between your knees, and let the other arm support your back. With a C shape, face into the opening so the curve supports your head, bump, and knees, or flip it so the spine of the C blocks your back. Give any new pillow a week before judging it. If you still drift onto your back, a firm wedge behind your lower back tips you toward your side, so you land tilted rather than flat.

When sleep belongs on your prenatal visit list

Accidentally sleeping on your back does not need reporting, treatment, or a night of worry. It is one of the most common anxieties of the third trimester, and the honest answer is reassuring: roll over and carry on. Guidance focuses on the going to sleep position precisely because it is the part you can control. Save your energy for the things that do warrant a conversation. If you cannot find any comfortable position for several nights running, if lying down regularly makes you feel faint or dizzy, or if new loud snoring appears, those are reasonable things to raise at your next appointment.

One thing is different and more urgent: your baby's movements. If you notice your baby moving less than usual, or the pattern changes, contact your midwife or maternity unit right away rather than waiting for a scheduled visit, whatever position you slept in. For everything else, a short note helps the appointment go further. Jot down which positions you have tried, how many nights sleep has been rough, and any question you keep meaning to ask; the BeMama app is a handy place to keep those notes with dates attached. Your midwife or doctor knows your pregnancy and can tailor position advice to you.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Many pregnancy symptoms are common, but severity, timing, and the effect on eating, drinking, breathing, sleep, or daily function matter. Comfort measures should be low risk and medicines should be checked with a prenatal professional.

A symptom that is severe, sudden, persistent, or accompanied by bleeding, fever, vision changes, chest pain, one-sided swelling, fainting, or reduced fetal movement needs prompt assessment rather than self-treatment.

How BeMama can help

Record when symptoms begin, what makes them better or worse, and related temperature, food, hydration, or activity in BeMama. The pattern can aid communication but cannot determine whether a symptom is normal.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, severe headache, vision changes, heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, fever, or inability to keep fluids down.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Morning Sickness: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy
  • ACOG — Problems of the Digestive System
  • CDC — Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • From 28 weeks, go to sleep on your side; the position you fall asleep in is the one that counts.
  • In the first trimester, any position that feels comfortable is fine, including your back and your stomach.
  • The left side is often suggested, but falling asleep on your right side is acceptable too.
  • Pillows between your knees, under your bump, and behind your back make side sleeping stick.
  • Waking on your back is normal, just roll over; contact your maternity team promptly if your baby's movements change.

Frequently asked questions

When should I stop sleeping on my back while pregnant?

Aim to stop falling asleep on your back from 28 weeks, the start of the third trimester. From that point, guidance links going to sleep on your back with reduced blood flow and a higher risk of stillbirth, and side sleeping avoids that pressure. If lying on your back already feels dizzy or unpleasant earlier, switch sooner. What matters is the position you settle into, not where you drift during the night.

Is it OK to sleep on my right side while pregnant?

Yes, sleeping on your right side is fine. The left side is often suggested first because it keeps the uterus off a large vein that sits slightly to the right of your spine, but guidance treats either side as safe for falling asleep. Switch sides whenever a hip or shoulder gets sore. A comfortable position you can hold beats a perfect one you cannot.

What happens if I accidentally sleep on my back while pregnant?

Nothing that needs fixing: just roll onto your side and go back to sleep. The advice is about the position you fall asleep in, because no one can control where they move overnight, and waking up on your back is common. Many people find their body wakes them with discomfort when they end up flat. If your baby's movements ever seem reduced or changed, contact your maternity team promptly, whatever position you slept in.

Can I sleep on my stomach while pregnant?

Yes, you can sleep on your stomach for as long as it feels comfortable, which is often well into the second trimester. The muscular wall of the uterus and the amniotic fluid cushion the baby, so front sleeping does not cause harm in early pregnancy. Most people give it up naturally as the bump grows. Use that transition to start practicing side sleeping before the 28 week advice begins.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
